stumbles.why: remex is never explained. It could be a library, a method or a prior project. Its hash cells (the hashing scheme, bits, number of cells) are not described, so the 70%/34% comparison can't be interpreted.

stumbles.quote: e-means makes those centroids cheap to train, and that is what it gives remex.
stumbles.why: e-means is not defined beyond a link to a page. We don't know how it differs from Lloyd's k-means, so the claim can't be assessed. The sentence also implies remex gets training speed, which the last paragraph undercuts.
Refers to earlier work by Oskar and the author that the text never describes. Oskar is also introduced without any context.

stumbles.quote: remex then applies its 1-bit quantization to that offset
stumbles.why: remex's 1-bit quantization is assumed known. It is unclear whether it means 1 bit per dimension, which the later 'second bit per dimension' suggests but never states.

stumbles.quote: the centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector
stumbles.why: The figure isn't derived. 4,096 centroids at 768 dimensions in float32 is about 12 MB, which is 126 bytes per vector at 100,000 vectors, but this is never shown. The unstated dimension and precision make it hard to follow. It also isn't clear why this cost is amortized per vector, or how it compares with a second bit per dimension.

The baseline isn't named. We can't tell whether 0.840 is plain 1-bit remex without residuals. It is also unclear how recall@10 relates to the earlier '90% of true neighbours' figure, or what search setup (nprobe, rerank) was used.

stumbles.quote: in 1 to 3 passes, 1.6 to 10.2 times sooner on 4 CPUs
stumbles.why: It's unclear what a 'pass' is, and why 1–3 passes can be compared with 25 Lloyd iterations. It also isn't said what the 1.6 to 10.2 range varies over, so the speedup is ambiguous.

stumbles.quote: I assumed the benefit would be training speed and spent the first hour measuring it.
stumbles.why: This seems to conflict with the opening claim that cheap training is what e-means gives remex. The text then says the result lay elsewhere, and the ending says the algorithm choice comes down to training time. The main finding is therefore unclear.

stumbles.quote: I had expected residual coding to be the main result and the index cells to be a footnote, and it came out the other way round.
stumbles.why: The first paragraph's claim is that the cells beat remex's hash cells, but the section never says that e-means rather than Lloyd's produced this. The last paragraph says both give the same recall, so e-means's contribution is only speed, which is confusing.

point: On 100,000 EmbeddingGemma vectors, k-means centroids used as index cells beat remex's hash cells (90% recall at 0.56% scanned versus 70% at 34%). Residual coding was a smaller win, and e-means matters only because it trains those centroids faster than Lloyd's.
